findings.claim_text: Aerobic respiration produces a large amount of energy (ATP) relative to the amount of glucose used — around 36–38 ATP molecules per glucose.
findings.issue: The 36–38 figure is the classic theoretical maximum. Modern biochemistry research puts the actual yield closer to 29–30 ATP per glucose in eukaryotic cells once transport costs into the mitochondria are accounted for. At GCSE level the 36–38 figure is the universally taught approximation and is on all Edexcel mark schemes, so this is not wrong for exam purposes, but it is a simplification of the current scientific consensus.
findings.correct_version: The textbook/GCSE-accepted value is 36–38 ATP. This is appropriate for GCSE Edexcel PE and matches mark scheme expectation. No change required.

findings.claim_text: The maximum heart rate is estimated by 220 minus age: a 16-year-old has a maximum of approximately 204 bpm.
findings.issue: The 220 − age formula is the universally accepted GCSE/Edexcel-specified formula and is correct for exam purposes. However, it is known to be inaccurate by ±10–20 bpm for many individuals; the more accurate Tanaka formula (208 − 0.7 × age) is preferred in sports science research. For a 16-year-old, 220 − 16 = 204 is arithmetically correct. No change needed for GCSE purposes, but this is an accepted simplification.
findings.correct_version: 220 − age = 204 for a 16-year-old is the Edexcel-specified formula and is correct for mark scheme purposes. No change required.

findings.claim_text: Elite endurance athletes such as distance cyclists or marathon runners can have resting heart rates of 40–50 bpm or even lower.
findings.issue: This is accurate. Typical endurance athlete resting heart rate is 40–60 bpm; some athletes (e.g. Miguel Indurain, reportedly 28 bpm) can go much lower. The claim 40–50 bpm 'or even lower' is correct.

findings.claim_text: The weight of the head — approximately 4–5 kg
findings.issue: The average adult human head weighs approximately 4.5–5 kg (commonly cited as about 5 kg / 11 lbs). The lesson's 4–5 kg range sits at the lower end but is broadly acceptable. Some sources cite it as closer to 5–6 kg. For a 15–16 year old student the lower range may be appropriate. Minor understatement at the lower end.
findings.correct_version: The average adult head weighs approximately 4.5–5.5 kg. Citing 4–5 kg is acceptable for GCSE level though slightly low at the bottom end. No material impact on the lever-system teaching point.

findings.lesson_title: Principles of Training and Programme Design
findings.claim_text: The aerobic training zone sits between 60% and 80% of maximum heart rate.
findings.issue: This is the standard Edexcel GCSE specification range. ACSM guidelines describe a moderate-to-vigorous zone of 50–85% of max HR (or 60–80% of heart rate reserve), with 60–80% of max HR falling within this and being appropriate as the aerobic development zone for GCSE teaching purposes. No error.
findings.correct_version: Accurate for Edexcel GCSE PE purposes. No change required.

findings.lesson_title: Principles of Training and Programme Design
findings.claim_text: The anaerobic training zone sits between 80% and 90% of maximum heart rate.
findings.issue: The 80–90% zone as the anaerobic zone is a conventional GCSE simplification. It is consistent with the Edexcel specification and the threshold generally accepted in educational contexts. Actual lactate threshold occurs at roughly 80–85% of HRmax in trained athletes. No material error.
findings.correct_version: Accurate for GCSE Edexcel PE purposes. No change required.

findings.claim_text: In a second-class lever, the classic sporting example is rising onto your toes (plantar flexion). The toes act as the fulcrum at the front of the foot, the body weight (load) acts through the ball of the foot, and the calf muscles (gastrocnemius) provide the effort at the back of the heel via the Achilles tendon.
findings.issue: This is slightly imprecise. In the toe-raise second-class lever: the fulcrum is at the metatarsophalangeal joints (where the toes meet the foot), the load is the body weight acting downward through the centre of the foot/ankle, and the effort is via the Achilles tendon to the calcaneus (heel bone) — the effort arm is the distance from the toes to the heel. Stating the effort acts 'at the back of the heel' is correct. However, saying body weight acts through 'the ball of the foot' is slightly inaccurate — body weight acts through the ankle/tibia above the foot, while the ball of the foot is between fulcrum and load application point. This is a nuanced teaching point; the description given is the conventional Edexcel simplification used in most GCSE resources and mark schemes.
findings.correct_version: The Edexcel-standard description of the toe-raise as a second-class lever is correct and consistent with the specification. The exact description of 'body weight through the ball of the foot' is a conventional simplification. No change required.

findings.claim_text: The Harvard Step Test requires the participant to step up and down on a 30 cm bench for 5 minutes at a set pace. One minute after stopping, the heart rate is measured.
findings.issue: TWO ISSUES. (1) Bench height: The standard Harvard Step Test protocol uses a 50 cm bench for men and 40 cm for women. 30 cm is a modified/school version for non-athletic populations, not the standard protocol. Edexcel GCSE PE resources commonly specify 30 cm as the school-adapted version, but some mark schemes reference the original 50 cm. The lesson should clarify this is the adapted GCSE version. (2) Heart rate timing: Heart rate in the standard Harvard Step Test is NOT measured at 1 minute after stopping. The standard protocol measures heart rate across three 30-second intervals: 1:00–1:30 min, 2:00–2:30 min, and 3:00–3:30 min post-exercise. The lesson says 'one minute after stopping, the heart rate is measured' — this conflates the first measurement window start time with a single measurement. A lower heart rate indicates fitness, but the 'one minute after stopping' description is a simplification that omits the protocol detail. At Edexcel GCSE level a single post-exercise heart rate reading is sometimes the simplified version taught, so this may be intentional simplification.
findings.correct_version: (1) Bench height: clarify this is the adapted school version (30 cm); the original Harvard Step Test uses 50 cm for men / 40 cm for women. (2) The standard protocol measures pulse in three 30-second windows during recovery (1:00–1:30, 2:00–2:30, 3:00–3:30 min). Some GCSE adaptations use a single reading 1 minute post-exercise. If this is the Edexcel-taught simplification, add a note that the full protocol uses three recovery readings.

findings.claim_text: The Illinois agility run test: the participant starts lying face down and, on the signal, sprints up and back along a course of cones placed 5 metres apart, weaving between cones in the middle section.
findings.issue: The '5 metres apart' claim is inaccurate for the weaving (central) cones. The Illinois agility test course is 10 m long × 5 m wide. The FOUR central weaving cones are spaced 3.3 metres apart (10 m ÷ 3 spaces), not 5 metres. The 5 metres refers to the width of the course (distance between the outer lanes), not the cone spacing in the weaving section. The starting position (lying face down / prone) is correctly described.
findings.correct_version: The course is 10 m long × 5 m wide. The four central weaving cones are spaced 3.3 m apart. Replace '5 metres apart' with '3.3 metres apart' when referring to the weaving cones. The 5 m figure describes the width of the rectangular course.

findings.lesson_title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
findings.claim_text: Vital capacity typically ranges from 3 to 6 litres depending on body size, sex and training status.
findings.issue: Most clinical and physiology references cite normal vital capacity as 3–5 litres (StatPearls / NIH, Physiopedia). The upper end of 6 litres slightly overstates the typical range for healthy adults, though very large/tall individuals or elite endurance athletes can exceed 5 litres. The commonly accepted range is 3–5 L. Citing up to 6 L risks students quoting this in exams where 3–5 L is the expected answer.
findings.correct_version: Change '3 to 6 litres' to '3 to 5 litres' as this reflects the standard clinical reference range. Note that highly trained athletes may exceed 5 L if desired.

findings.claim_text: Beta blockers ... are used in precision sports such as archery, shooting and snooker. Health risks include lowered blood pressure and bradycardia.
findings.issue: WADA's Prohibited List bans beta blockers in Archery (WA), Automobile (FIA), Billiards — all disciplines (WCBS), Darts (WDF), Golf (IGF), Mini-Golf (WMF), and Shooting (ISSF, IPC). Snooker is governed by WCBS (World Confederation of Billiards Sports), which covers all billiards/cue sports including snooker. So snooker IS covered by the billiards category. However, the lesson in Unit 1 (Lesson 16) also lists snooker alongside archery and shooting, and adds 'snooker' explicitly. The issue is that the first lesson (L16) in the fitness unit also lists beta blockers as used 'in precision sports such as archery, shooting and snooker' which is broadly correct. The health effects listed — 'lowered blood pressure and bradycardia' — are correct.
findings.correct_version: Snooker falls under WADA's Billiards (WCBS) category so the listing is effectively correct. The description of health risks (bradycardia, lowered blood pressure) is accurate. No critical change required. For precision, could note that snooker falls under the 'billiards' category of the WADA prohibited list.

findings.lesson_title: Injury Prevention, PARQ, RICE and PEDs
findings.claim_text: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a peptide hormone produced naturally by the kidneys that stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells
findings.issue: The claim that EPO is 'produced naturally by the kidneys' is correct for adults — the kidneys (peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex) are the primary site of EPO production in adults. The liver is a secondary extrarenal site. However, the lesson in the Health unit (L11) describes EPO as produced by 'bone marrow' — this is an error. EPO stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells, but EPO itself is made primarily by the kidneys. The lesson in L16 correctly attributes EPO production to the kidneys. Check L11 description.
findings.correct_version: L16 correctly states EPO is produced by the kidneys. This is accurate. No change needed for L16.

findings.claim_text: The World Health Organization defines health as a state of complete physical, emotional and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
findings.issue: The original 1948 WHO definition uses 'mental' not 'emotional': 'Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' The Edexcel GCSE PE specification substitutes 'emotional' for 'mental' throughout, which is a deliberate specification-level word choice. Using 'emotional' is consistent with the Edexcel specification document and all Edexcel mark schemes. No error from the spec's perspective, but differs from the WHO source definition.
findings.correct_version: The Edexcel specification uses 'emotional' not 'mental' — this is correct and intentional for Edexcel mark schemes. The WHO original says 'mental'. For GCSE PE purposes the lesson wording is correct. No change required.

findings.claim_text: Carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, further reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
findings.issue: Accurate. CO binds haemoglobin with affinity 200–270 times greater than oxygen (multiple sources confirm this range). The lesson in Lesson 19 collapsible puts the figure at 'an affinity 200 times greater than oxygen' — this is within the verified range (200–270x). No error.
findings.correct_version: Accurate. The 200x figure cited elsewhere in the lesson is within the 200–270x verified range. No change required.

findings.claim_text: Even mild dehydration — a loss of just 2% of body water — measurably impairs aerobic performance and decision-making ability.
findings.issue: This is the widely cited threshold (≥2% body mass loss impairing aerobic performance). The scientific consensus supports this threshold, though some more recent research under time-trial conditions found impairment may not occur until 3–4% loss under certain conditions. The 2% figure is widely used in ACSM guidelines and GCSE PE resources. No material error.
findings.correct_version: Accurate for GCSE PE purposes and consistent with ACSM guidance. No change required.

findings.claim_text: Water makes up around 60% of adult body mass
findings.issue: 60% is the standard average cited for adult males. For adult females it is closer to 50–55% due to higher average body fat. The '60%' figure is commonly used as the general average and is correct for general teaching purposes.
findings.correct_version: Accurate general figure. No change required.
